module.title: Deep Learning & NLP
module.subtitle: Neural networks, a PyTorch loop, and how transformers changed language work.
module.description: Build the bridge from classical ML to modern language models. Learn what a neural network optimizes, write a training loop you can debug, and understand tokenization, embeddings and attention well enough to choose the right tool.
outcomes: Explain layers, activations, loss, backpropagation and overfitting without hiding behind frameworks.
Write and debug a PyTorch training loop with train/validation separation.
Choose between classical text models, fine-tuned transformers and prompted LLMs for a task.

lessons.title: Neural networks from one neuron to backprop
lessons.summary: What a network actually learns, why non-linearity matters, and how training goes wrong.
lessons.body_html:
A neural network is a stack of learned transformations. Each layer takes a vector, multiplies it by a weight matrix, adds a bias, and applies a non-linear activation. Stack enough layers and the network can represent complex functions.

One neuron

output = activation(w1*x1 + w2*x2 + ... + b)

Without a non-linear activation, stacked layers collapse into one linear transformation. ReLU is a common default: it returns the input if positive and zero otherwise. It is cheap and helps gradients flow.

Loss and learning

The loss measures how wrong the output is. Cross-entropy is standard for classification; mean squared error for regression. Backpropagation computes how each weight contributed to the loss, and an optimizer such as Adam or SGD updates the weights.

for epoch in range(epochs):
    for xb, yb in train_loader:
        optimizer.zero_grad()
        logits = model(xb)
        loss = loss_fn(logits, yb)
        loss.backward()
        optimizer.step()

Epochs, batches, and learning rate

An epoch is one pass over the training set. A batch is a small group of examples processed together. The learning rate controls step size. Too high and the loss explodes; too low and training never converges. These are the first knobs to inspect.

Overfitting

Training loss going down while validation loss goes up is the classic overfitting signal. Early stopping, weight decay, dropout, data augmentation, and simpler models are the usual responses. More epochs are not automatically better.

When not to use deep learning: small tabular datasets with strong features often favor gradient boosting or linear models. Deep learning earns its cost with large data, unstructured inputs, or transfer learning from a pretrained model.
takeaways: Non-linear activations are what let stacked layers represent complex functions.
Training minimizes a loss through backpropagation and an optimizer.
Training loss falling while validation loss rises is the overfitting signal.
lessons.practice: Sketch a two-layer network for a tabular input and label the shapes at every step. Success: you can explain why removing the activation collapses the model into a linear function.

lessons.title: A PyTorch training loop you can trust
lessons.summary: Datasets, loaders, train and eval modes, metrics, checkpoints, and the checks that catch silent bugs.
lessons.body_html:
A training loop is a small state machine. Keep it boring, explicit, and instrumented. If you cannot tell whether the model is learning after one epoch, the loop is hiding something.

Dataset and DataLoader

from torch.utils.data import Dataset, DataLoader

class TicketDataset(Dataset):
    def __init__(self, texts, labels, tokenizer, max_length=256):
        self.encodings = tokenizer(
            texts, truncation=True, max_length=max_length, padding=True
        )
        self.labels = labels

    def __len__(self):
        return len(self.labels)

    def __getitem__(self, index):
        item = {key: value[index] for key, value in self.encodings.items()}
        item["labels"] = self.labels[index]
        return item

loader = DataLoader(dataset, batch_size=16, shuffle=True)

The DataLoader handles batching and shuffling. For text, the tokenizer turns strings into token IDs and attention masks. Keep padding and truncation policy explicit.

The loop

model.train()
for batch in train_loader:
    batch = {k: v.to(device) for k, v in batch.items()}
    optimizer.zero_grad()
    outputs = model(**batch)
    loss = outputs.loss
    loss.backward()
    optimizer.step()

Then evaluate:

model.eval()
with torch.no_grad():
    for batch in valid_loader:
        outputs = model(**batch)
        predictions = outputs.logits.argmax(dim=-1)

model.eval() changes dropout and batch-normalization behavior. Forgetting it makes validation noisy and misleading.

Check the silent bugs

  • Print the loss for the first few batches. Is it near the expected random baseline?
  • Overfit a tiny subset on purpose. If the model cannot memorize ten examples, the loop or labels are wrong.
  • Compare label distribution and prediction distribution. A model that predicts one class is not learning.
  • Save the checkpoint and reload it before trusting a score.
Habit: a training script without a fixed seed, a validation split, and saved metrics is an anecdote, not an experiment.
takeaways: Dataset and DataLoader separate data handling from the training loop.
model.train() and model.eval() change dropout and batch-normalization behaviour.
Overfit a tiny batch on purpose to prove the loop and labels work.
lessons.practice: Write a training loop, overfit ten examples to near-zero loss, then evaluate on a validation split. Success: you can show the memorization curve and the generalization gap.

lessons.title: From words to transformers
lessons.summary: Tokenization, embeddings, attention, and the decision between classical NLP, fine-tuning and prompting.
lessons.body_html:
Language models do not see words; they see tokens. A tokenizer splits text into subword units, maps them to integer IDs, and the model learns a vector for each ID. Common words may be one token; rare words split into pieces.

Embeddings

An embedding maps a token to a dense vector. During pretraining, tokens that appear in similar contexts end up with similar vectors. Sentence embeddings extend the idea to whole passages and power semantic search.

Attention

Self-attention lets each token weigh information from other tokens. The model learns which parts of the context matter for the current prediction. Stacked attention layers and feed-forward blocks produce contextual representations.

“The bank raised its rates.”
“We sat by the river bank.”

The token “bank” gets different contextual representations because attention incorporates the surrounding words.

Three levels of reuse

  • Classical NLP — TF-IDF, logistic regression, gradient boosting. Fast, strong baselines for small labelled datasets.
  • Fine-tuning — adapt a pretrained transformer to your labelled task. More compute and data than a baseline, often excellent for classification and extraction.
  • Prompting an LLM — no task-specific training; best when the task is open-ended, labelled data is scarce, or you need generation and reasoning.

Choosing

Start with a cheap baseline, then fine-tune if the error analysis shows a representation problem. Use an LLM when the task needs language understanding or generation that a small supervised model cannot provide, and you can evaluate the output. “We used a transformer” is not a rationale.

Evaluation: for classification, use per-class precision and recall, not just accuracy. For generation, evaluate task-specific qualities and safety, not only fluency.
takeaways: Tokenization turns text into IDs; embeddings and attention build context.
Classical NLP, fine-tuning and prompting are different cost/data trade-offs.
Evaluate the task, not fluency alone.
lessons.practice: Take 20 support tickets, label them manually, and compare a keyword baseline with an LLM prompt. Success: you can name the per-class errors and which approach you would ship.

lessons.title: Applied deep dive: a text classifier from baseline to transformer
lessons.summary: A complete comparison workflow: TF-IDF baseline, fine-tuning, confidence routing and error analysis.
lessons.body_html:
Text classification is the best first deep-learning project because the baseline is cheap and the failure analysis is visible.

1. Baseline first

from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline

baseline = Pipeline([
    ("tfidf", TfidfVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, 2), min_df=2)),
    ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced")),
])
baseline.fit(train_texts, train_labels)

Record per-class precision, recall and the confusion matrix. This is the number the transformer must beat to justify its cost.

2. Fine-tune a small transformer

from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
import torch

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("distilbert-base-uncased")
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
    "distilbert-base-uncased", num_labels=4
)

batch = tokenizer(train_texts[:16], truncation=True, padding=True, return_tensors="pt")
labels = torch.tensor(train_labels[:16])
outputs = model(**batch, labels=labels)
loss = outputs.loss
loss.backward()  # after optimizer.zero_grad() in the real loop

Use a validation split, early stopping and a fixed seed. Keep the baseline evaluation script so the comparison is reproducible.

3. Confidence routing

probabilities = torch.softmax(outputs.logits, dim=-1)
confidence, predicted = probabilities.max(dim=-1)
route = ["human" if c < 0.6 else "model" for c in confidence.tolist()]

A confident wrong answer is worse than an uncertain one sent to a human. Measure coverage (how many tickets the model handles) against accuracy on the covered set.

4. Error analysis

Read at least 20 misclassified examples. Label the cause: ambiguous label, missing context, label noise, domain shift, or model limitation. If the labels are inconsistent, a bigger model will learn the noise.

5. Compare honestly

ApproachCostStrengthFailure
TF-IDF + linearLowFast, strong baseline, interpretableMisses nuanced language
Fine-tuned transformerMediumBetter language understandingNeeds data, compute and care
Prompted LLMPer callNo training, flexibleCost, latency, variability
Portfolio proof: show the baseline and transformer side by side, with a cost/quality decision. “Transformer won by 0.4%” may mean the baseline should ship.
takeaways: A strong classical baseline makes the deep-learning decision honest.
Confidence routing is a product feature that turns uncertainty into a human workflow.
Error analysis on real mistakes is more valuable than another architecture.
lessons.practice: Train a TF-IDF baseline on a small labelled set, inspect 10 errors, then decide whether fine-tuning is justified. Success: the decision cites a metric and a cost.

lessons.title: Embeddings and semantic search
lessons.summary: How vectors turn meaning into a search index, and how to evaluate retrieval before adding an LLM.
lessons.body_html:
An embedding maps text to a vector. Similar meanings end up close together, which lets you search by intent instead of exact keywords. This is the retrieval half of RAG and a useful product feature on its own.

Cosine similarity

import numpy as np

def cosine(a, b):
    a, b = np.array(a), np.array(b)
    return float(a @ b / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)))

Cosine compares direction, not magnitude. Normalize vectors once if you will compare many of them; then the dot product is enough.

Build a tiny index

def search(query_vector, vectors, items, k=3):
    scores = [cosine(query_vector, vector) for vector in vectors]
    ranked = sorted(range(len(items)), key=lambda i: scores[i], reverse=True)
    return [(items[i], scores[i]) for i in ranked[:k]]

For a local prototype this is enough. At scale, use an approximate nearest-neighbour index and measure the quality/latency trade-off.

Chunk before embedding

Embed passages, not entire documents. Chunks should carry a source id, position and enough context to stand alone. Overlap preserves boundary context but duplicates results if it is too large.

Evaluate retrieval

  • Recall@k — did the right passage appear in the top k?
  • MRR — how high did the first relevant result rank?
  • Slice analysis — exact names, numbers, code and long-tail vocabulary often fail.

Before adding a reranker or an LLM, inspect 20 retrieval failures. You may need better chunking, hybrid keyword search or a different embedding model.

Common trap: judging retrieval by the final chatbot answer. If retrieval missed the evidence, a better prompt cannot save it.
takeaways: Embeddings support semantic search but still need chunking and provenance.
Hybrid keyword + semantic retrieval often beats either alone.
lessons.practice: Embed 20 short passages, run 10 queries and compute recall@3 by hand. Success: you can name the queries where semantic search failed and why.

questions.prompt: What does a single artificial neuron compute?
choices: A random number independent of the input.
A weighted sum of inputs plus a bias, passed through an activation function.
A database query.
A tokenizer.
questions.explanation: The neuron computes a linear combination and applies a non-linearity. Stacking these creates the representational power of a neural network.

choices: It makes the model train faster.
It disables training-specific behavior such as dropout and changes batch-normalization behavior.
It increases the learning rate.
It converts the model to a different language.
questions.explanation: Dropout is active in training mode and would make validation noisy. Eval mode gives deterministic, deployment-like behavior.

questions.prompt: What is the main job of a DataLoader?
choices: To train the model.
To batch, shuffle and feed examples efficiently to the training loop.
To compute the loss.
To tokenize text.
questions.explanation: The DataLoader wraps a Dataset and handles batching, shuffling, and loading. Tokenization belongs in the Dataset or preprocessing step.

questions.prompt: What does self-attention let a transformer do?
choices: Compress the model to one layer.
Weigh information from different tokens in the context when building each token's representation.
Avoid tokenization entirely.
Guarantee factual correctness.
questions.explanation: Attention learns which context positions matter for each token. It is why the same word can have different representations in different sentences.

questions.prompt: Training loss falls while validation loss rises. What is the best interpretation?
choices: The model is underfitting.
The model is overfitting; it is memorizing training data rather than generalizing.
The validation set is always wrong.
The learning rate is too low.
questions.explanation: Diverging losses are the signature of overfitting. Use early stopping, regularization, more data, or a simpler model, and check for leakage.

questions.prompt: You have 2,000 labelled support tickets and need a category classifier. What is the most sensible first experiment?
choices: Train a large language model from scratch.
Build a TF-IDF + linear baseline, then compare a fine-tuned small transformer if the baseline's errors justify it.
Skip evaluation and ship the first transformer.
Use an agent framework.
questions.explanation: With modest labelled data, a classical baseline is fast and strong. Fine-tuning is justified by measured errors, not by novelty.

flashcards.front: Why do neural networks need non-linear activations?
flashcards.back: Without them, stacked linear layers collapse into a single linear transformation. Non-linearities let the network represent complex relationships.

flashcards.front: What do model.train() and model.eval() change?
flashcards.back: They switch training-specific layers such as dropout and batch normalization. Always evaluate in eval mode with gradients disabled.
A unit produced by a tokenizer — often a word piece. The model maps tokens to IDs and learns embeddings for them. Token counts drive context limits and API cost.

Fine-tuning updates model weights on labelled examples for a specific task. Prompting uses a frozen model with instructions and context. Start with prompting when labels are scarce; fine-tune when you need consistent task behavior and have data.

flashcards.front: How do you detect overfitting in a training loop?
flashcards.back: Track training and validation loss each epoch. If validation loss rises while training loss falls, the model is memorizing. Use early stopping, regularization, augmentation, or more data.
